The reviewer describes a wheel-spin feature (the 'genie game') inside this casino-slot game. The wheel visibly stops on a large prize, but then a genie animation moves the wheel onward to a 'spin' tag, and the final payout is much lower than what the wheel appeared to land on (100 million with a 5x multiplier drops to 48 million). The core complaint is that the shown outcome is overridden by an animation the player cannot control, so the displayed result is not the real result. This is a claim that the game conceals or manipulates how an outcome is determined rather than a matter of ordinary unlucky spins. The request that the player be given a choice to keep or spin is a suggestion for an absent feature and codes nothing. No real-money wager is described, so Gambling does not apply.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: whe the wheel spin after stopping on a great price the genie move the wheel to a spin tag, and then the prices after the spin are way lower than the original price, from 100 million with 5x multiplier to a 48 million
labels.rule_applied: Boundary rule vs alleged rigging: 'Assign where the span asserts that the game conceals or manipulates the determination of outcomes... engineered near-misses'
labels.rationale: The wheel visibly stops on a high prize only for the genie to move it to a lower one; the reviewer asserts the game manipulates the outcome after the fact, hiding the true result from the player.

The reviewer is describing end-game PvP in Clash Royale. The whole complaint is against other players they face after 8,000 trophies, specifically certain card archetypes that feel oppressive to defend. They also assert the game is 'pay to win': that reaching higher ranks requires money rather than skill, and that updates keep making it more pay-to-win by buffing unpopular cards. No social, psychological, or temporal mechanics beyond that are described. The 'buff cards people hate' remark is about meta balance, not devaluation of items the player already purchased, so Power Creep does not apply.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: its also pay to win and usually doesn't let you get higher from just using skill
labels.rule_applied: Pay to Win [low-level] under Pay to Progress
labels.rationale: The span asserts that money, rather than skill, is what lets the player advance to higher ranks, i.e. payment grants the advantage of progression.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: all you play against after 8k trophies is mega knight,pekka, and golem
labels.rule_applied: definition
labels.rationale: The reviewer describes the core loop of facing other players on a ladder, which is competition against other players.

parsed.analysis: The review has three distinct threads. First, a customer-service complaint: 9 diamonds were spent but a game element did not appear within the original 5 moves plus 5 purchased additional moves, and support would not refund. This describes a lost purchase and a support refusal; it does not clearly describe a designed dark pattern behind it, so I will not assign from it. Second, a monetization remark: 'you don't have to pay to win' explicitly negates pay-to-win, and 'don't buy from this game beyond the pass' names a pass as the only purchase the reviewer still tolerates but does not describe what the pass does or how it operates, so no Recurring Fee mechanic is carried by the span. Third, a social feature: 'Get friends and a team and trade lives' describes exchanging lives with people already in the player's friend and team circle, which is a resource-transfer mechanism between current players.

labels.label: S_Reciprocity
labels.span: Get friends and a team and trade lives.
labels.rule_applied: definition (Alt. def.) 'Feeling obligated to return a favor, share resources, trade an item, etc.' and the Reciprocity vs Forced Fellowship boundary
labels.rationale: Trading lives with friends and team members already playing is an in-game resource-exchange mechanic between existing players, not recruitment of new players, so it codes Reciprocity.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes three aspects of the game: life regeneration requiring a wait, daily login prizes that reset after a missed day, and some small celebratory tasks they find unnecessary. The last item is an evaluation of content quality and codes nothing. The first two are framed as suggestions for change, but each references an existing design behaviour — lives refill on a real-time timer (the reviewer wishes it were shorter) and daily prizes restart when a day is missed. Under R12, the suggestions name the currently present mechanics they would alter, so both are codable.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: maybe only 5-10 minutes for a new life
labels.rule_applied: Wait to Play: patterns that impose arbitrary wait times on players through in-game timers; lives/energy refilling over time
labels.rationale: The span implies lives are gated behind a real-time refill timer that is longer than 5-10 minutes, an arbitrary wait imposed by the game's clock.

labels.label: T_DailyRewards
labels.span: just because you miss a day doesnt mean that you need to start over on your daily prizes
labels.rule_applied: definition: penalising players for failing to log in daily
labels.rationale: The span describes daily prizes with an active penalty — restarting from the beginning — for missing a day, which is a daily login incentive with a missed-day consequence.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing what happens inside the game when an advertisement plays. They report that after seeing an ad there is no way to close it: no close (cross) control is provided, tapping anywhere on the screen navigates to an app store, and pressing back leaves the ad stuck on screen so the only exit is killing the game process. This is an in-game ad-viewing experience that the player cannot dismiss, i.e., the player is compelled to watch or endure the ad and cannot end the session at a moment of their choosing through ordinary means. The review attributes this to the ad's design (missing close control), not to a crash or technical fault.

labels.label: T_Advertisement
labels.span: there is no way to close it. No cross mark on the screen , if you try to click anywhere on the screen it takes you to store. If you go back to game it is still stuck in the last sceeen of the ad. You have to kill the game to come out of the ad screen
labels.rule_applied: Definition: 'Compelled to view advertisements or incentivized to do so through the promise of rewards.'
labels.rationale: The ad shown in the game cannot be dismissed through any in-ad control, back navigation leaves it stuck, and only killing the game exits it, so the player is compelled to view the advertisement.

The review has two distinct parts. The first describes purchasing Poké Balls and then finding that Pokémon 'keep breaking out' of them, so the player consumes balls faster and must buy more, ending with 'I feel taken advantage of.' This is an accusation that the game manipulates catch outcomes (higher break-out rates after spending) to drive continued purchases. The second part, added as an edit, denies authorship entirely: 'I DID NOT WRITE THIS REVIEW... I DO NOT KNOW ANYONE' - a claim that a review appeared under the player's account that they did not author, which is the impersonation pattern of a review written under the player's identity.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: since I started purchasing, items "poke" balls that when I tried to make a capture that they keep breaking out so I go through the balls faster so I have to purchase more
labels.rule_applied: Illusion of Control boundary rule: assign where the span asserts that the game conceals or manipulates the determination of outcomes or tunes difficulty on a hidden schedule.
labels.rationale: The reviewer asserts that captures began failing more often once they started purchasing, a manipulation of the outcome determination engineered to consume purchased balls and drive further spending.

labels.label: S_FriendSpamImpersonation

labels.rule_applied: Friend Spam / Impersonation indicator: a store review written under the player's account assigns the label regardless of destination.
labels.rationale: The player states a review is attributed to them that they did not write and could not have written, i.e., content published under the player's identity without their authorship.

The reviewer describes a timed in-game event. They were a few steps short of a dice reward, ran out of dice, saw a countdown of '2 Days left', and when they logged back in after sleeping the event had been replaced, so the nearly-earned reward was lost. The mechanic operating here is the event clock: a reward is forfeited because the player could not play within the window the game set. The dice the reward pays out and the running out of dice are incidental to that loss. No monetary transaction is described, and the player actually quit rather than being pulled to keep playing, so retention-oriented psychological tags do not fit.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: The latest event I was about to get 525 dice as reward, I had 3 left to go and I ran out of dice, it said 2Days left. Now just logged in after sleeping and the event is now changed.
labels.rule_applied: definition (Wait to Play / event schedule): patterns that force players to adhere to the game's schedule, where a reward is lost because the event window passed while the player was away
labels.rationale: The event runs on the game's own clock ('it said 2Days left'); the reward of 525 dice was forfeited because the player could not complete the task within that window and the event ended while they slept, i.e., an appointment whose expiry the player had no control over.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer reports several distinct frustrations in MONOPOLY GO!. First, that the game stopped rewarding them for inviting friends to join through Facebook, which names the game's friend-invitation incentive even as the reviewer complains it is no longer paying out. Second, a shortage of dice, and an unlucky stretch at maximum bet with no shutdowns or bank heists, which reads as a losing run rather than a mechanistic claim about rigging. Third, sticker packs delivering duplicates, which describes a randomized reward delivery that prevents completing the sticker collection. Finally, a login/connection failure, which the reviewer attributes to a technical fault and is therefore not coded as a dark pattern.

labels.label: S_ForcedFellowship
labels.span: I get no rewards for inviting friends and getting them to join facebook
labels.rule_applied: Social Pyramid Scheme indicator
labels.rationale: The game incentivizes the player to invite friends to join through Facebook in exchange for rewards; the reviewer's complaint that the reward stopped confirms the invitation-recruitment mechanic exists.

labels.label: P_CompleteTheCollection
labels.span: Stickers are duplicates all the way
labels.rule_applied: definition
labels.rationale: The reviewer is working toward a sticker set and frames the repeated duplicates as blocking collection, which capitalizes on the drive to complete collections.

labels.label: P_RewardMania
labels.span: Stickers are duplicates all the way
labels.rule_applied: Variable Rewards indicator
labels.rationale: Duplicate sticker drops from a randomized pack pool describe unpredictable reward delivery that withholds the wanted item across repeated attempts.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a UI behaviour in the 1v1 betting lobby: every time the player opens the game or the 1v1 section, the interface automatically scrolls to and pre-selects the highest-stakes table the player can afford. The stated purpose is to induce accidental mis-clicks, drain the player's coins, and force them to buy more with real money. The core mechanic is an interface that defaults the player onto a harmful option with no opt-out, framed explicitly as a 'Dark UX' trick. The coins themselves are the player's in-game holdings, and losing them is described as forcing a real-money purchase of coins to keep going. I will not code Mandatory Marathon because the review describes the pre-selection causing the loss, not an inability to exit a session.

labels.label: M_UIMisdirection
labels.span: Every time you open the game or go to the 1v1 section, it automatically scrolls and selects the highest possible bet table based on your coins
labels.rule_applied: UI Misdirection boundary rule: a control or default that routes the player onto a harmful option, directing the interface against the player's intent.
labels.rationale: The interface pre-selects and auto-scrolls to the highest bet as a default, an opt-in arrangement the player must actively fight to avoid, which is an interface element directing the player toward a damaging selection.

labels.label: M_IntermediateCurrency
labels.span: so players lose all their hard-earned coins and are forced to buy real ones
labels.rule_applied: Premium Currency indicator: real money exchanged for in-game coins.
labels.rationale: The span shows the in-game coins being lost and then replenished by buying them with real money, establishing coins as a purchased intermediate currency.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: so players lose all their hard-earned coins and are forced to buy real ones
labels.rule_applied: definition: spending money required to keep progressing/playing the game.
labels.rationale: Being drained of all coins through the trick leaves the player unable to keep playing and 'forced to buy' coins, making continued play contingent on payment.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing the late-game economy of a coin-based solitaire game. Three things are present. First, an assertion that the game's randomness is rigged against the player ('the rng is so obviously against you'), i.e., outcomes are manipulated rather than fair. Second, a contrast between playing for free and spending money: playing without spending is stated to be unrewarding, which implies the paid path is what makes continued play viable. Third, a concrete economy rule that grounds that contrast: entering a level at around level 100 costs 2200 and even a win barely recovers that cost, so the player's resource balance drains the further they get, which is what pushes them toward spending money to keep going. There is no mention of a scheduled appointment, ad viewing, repetitive grinding, collections, or any other pattern.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: the rng is so obviously against you it's crazy
labels.rule_applied: P_IllusionOfControl boundary rule vs alleged rigging
labels.rationale: The reviewer asserts that the game conceals and manipulates the determination of outcomes, that the deal or difficulty is non-random and set against the player, which is the alleged-rigging form of the label.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: it's not rewarding playing the game without spending actual money.. at around level 100 it costs 2200 but if you win the level you'll barely make that back
labels.rule_applied: Pay to Progress free-alternative boundary rule
labels.rationale: The span contrasts playing without spending with an implicit paid alternative, and grounds it in an economy where the entry cost of a level exceeds even a winning payout, so the free path drains resources and cannot sustain further play without payment.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a base-builder game where community events are decided entirely by spending power rather than skill or gameplay. The key complaint is that winning an event requires a staggering real-money outlay (30k), so a free player has no chance. This is an explicit pay-to-win structure applied to inter-player competition in events.

labels.rule_applied: Pay to Win indicator
labels.rationale: The span states that winning game events is achieved through spending rather than skill, with a massive stated price for victory; a general (free) player cannot win.

labels.label: S_Competition

labels.rule_applied: definition (makes players against each other in competition)
labels.rationale: The events are player-against-player contests whose winners are determined by spending; the reviewer compares paid and free players in the same competitive arena.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a change to the game's bingo and daily rewards. The core complaint is that the daily reward is now only obtainable by wagering 50,000 in the casino, while the free route ('timed rewards') tops out at 40,000. The reviewer states they will not pay just to obtain the daily reward and will delete the game. Reading the implied design: the daily-reward goal sets a wager threshold above what free play can deliver, leaving payment (buying more coins to bet with) as the only way to close the gap. The reviewer does not describe missing a day or a login-calendar penalty, so the daily-return/streak mechanic of Daily Rewards is not what is being described; the mechanic at issue is a reward goal that cannot be met without spending money.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes arriving at the game with a full bag and coins earned and purchased, only to return after being away and find the bag empty and the coins consumed. This makes disengagement the moment of loss and raises the cost of leaving the game for any length of time. The underlying design appears to be one where the player must return in order to protect what they hold.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes an inventory-capacity wall. At level 34 they run out of board and refrigerator slots. Many of the occupied slots hold generator parts, lower-level generators awaiting merge, or high-level items (corn, lambchop, chicken pie) they refuse to discard. parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing a collection mechanic: completing an album for a grand prize, needing the last two cards. To finish, they bought a paid deal that was represented as guaranteeing NEW (previously unowned) cards, but the deal delivered duplicates instead. That failure is what they call a scam. Reading through it, the purchase is a stake paid into a reward delivery whose outcome is random: the deal could produce cards the player already owns rather than the missing ones. So the paid deal is a chance mechanic (Gambling), the delivery of cards from a randomized pool producing duplicates is Reward Mania, and the whole effort is framed around completing a set (Complete the Collection). The purchase does not unlock content outside the wager; it is itself a wager on a random draw, so Pay to Progress does not attach under the Gambling boundary rule.

labels.rule_applied: definition
labels.rationale: Real money was spent on a deal whose outcome is chance-based: it could return duplicate cards already owned rather than the promised missing ones, so the wager decided the reward.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes three intertwined things about Genshin Impact over time. First, rewards per patch shrink. Second, the meta (which characters are effective in damage-dealing content) shifts patch over patch, so staying effective means obtaining newly released characters. Third, they call the resulting dynamic pay-to-win. The pull mechanic is the gacha delivery system through which new characters are obtained, and the reviewer states that effective damage now depends on acquiring recent characters, which implies older holdings lose value. The quest-background complaint is an aesthetic/quality gripe with no manipulative design and is not coded. The 'pay 2 win' line plus needing new characters for damage is a payment-for-advantage claim. Reward Mania attaches to the named pull mechanic regardless of any monetary stake, since no stake is described.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer makes three distinct complaints. First, that the game differs from its advertisements and is actually 'a base growth simulator teeming with micro transaction menus' - the mismatch with advertised content is out-of-game marketing material, outside the coding unit, and the abundance of micro-transaction menus alone is a description of purchase volume, not of any friction-reducing interface mechanism, so no Technical or Easy to Purchase label follows from it. Second, that after a certain point 'players are encouraged to attack each other' - this is player-versus-player base raiding, ordinary competitive design where players are set against one another; nothing in the span describes asymmetric or dishonest conduct being incentivised (bullying, deception, exploiting players who cannot respond), so it codes Competition rather than Encourages Anti-Social Behavior. Third, 'there's a huge gap between p2w and f2p' - spending players hold a decisive advantage over free players, which is the Pay to Win indicator of Pay to Progress.

parsed.analysis: The review's core complaint is that a recent update removed a player-versus-player element called 'open silver' (a PvP mode for raiding silver), leaving the game as farming only. Within that account, the reviewer states that meaningful growth (game progression) is contingent on spending money, and then describes that paid growth as retroactively pointless because the update stripped out the PvP that gave it purpose. The removal of a feature is itself a design change rather than a dark pattern, but the spent-money-for-progress made worthless by the update shows value of purchases declining after acquisition is the Power Creep pattern.

labels.rationale: The span states that further meaningful progress is contingent on making a payment, meeting the Pay Wall indicator.
